opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a very gut-level decision at the time. I had the Bridgewater offer, which on paper was the "sensible" choice. It's a prestigious place, it pays well, and a lot of people around me saw it as a clear signal of where a career could go. But when I found out I was on the waitlist for Ken's program, I realized how much I actually wanted it, almost more than I wanted to admit to myself.

Part of it was that research math was the thing I kept coming back to. I loved number theory, and Ken is someone whose work I had read and admired. The idea of spending a summer doing real problems, not textbook exercises, with someone like that, and with other students who were just as obsessed, felt like a rare window. An internship at a finance firm would still be there in some form later. A chance to do serious research as an undergraduate, under that kind of mentorship, felt much more time-sensitive.

Being on the waitlist also clarified things for me. When something is uncertain, you find out how much you care about it. I was checking my email constantly and imagining what problems I'd work on. That told me something. If I was that excited about a maybe, I should probably follow it.

And looking back, it really shaped how I think about choices. The research experience taught me how to sit with a hard problem for a long time without knowing whether it would work out, how to build intuition, and how to collaborate. That turned out to matter much more for what I ended up doing than whatever I would have learned that summer in finance. So I'd say it was less about rejecting one path and more about choosing the thing that was genuinely mine.

r001.rationale: She says being waitlisted made her realize how much she wanted the program, and that her excitement about an uncertain possibility told her to pursue it.

r002.rationale: She describes the research opportunity as time-sensitive, but does not say she feared her admission chances would be worse the following summer.

fable-5.1.text:
So the honest answer is that it wasn't really a rational decision at first, it was more like an emotional one. I had already accepted the Bridgewater offer, and at that time, for a sophomore at MIT, that was kind of the dream. Everyone around me thought it was the obvious choice, and I think a part of me thought so too.

Then I got the email from Ken Ono's program saying I was on the waitlist. And I remember my first reaction was not disappointment, it was this weird surge of wanting it. Like, I hadn't realized how much I cared until I was told I might not get it. That told me something. If I had gotten rejected from Bridgewater, I don't think I would have felt that way. I would have felt bad for a day and moved on.

The other thing is that being on the waitlist made me take a hard look at what the summer would actually be. At Bridgewater I would be learning a lot, and the people are extremely smart, but I would be applying tools other people had already built, to problems other people had already framed. With Ken's program, the whole point was that you sit with a problem nobody knows the answer to, for weeks, and most of the time you fail. And I realized I had never really done that. I had done a lot of competitions, a lot of courses, but I had never produced a piece of mathematics that didn't exist before.

And there was a scarcity thing too. Bridgewater would still be there. If I wanted to go into finance, that door opens again at junior year, at senior year, after a PhD. But the chance to do real research with someone like Ken as a nineteen-year-old, that's not a door that stays open. So when a spot eventually opened up, I called Bridgewater and told them I was withdrawing. It was a very awkward phone call. But in hindsight that summer was probably the single decision that put me on the path I'm on now.

r001.rationale: She says being waitlisted triggered a surge of wanting the program and made her realize how much she cared, in the context of pursuing original mathematical research.

r002.rationale: She says the chance to do research as a nineteen-year-old might not stay open, but does not say she feared her admission chances would be worse the following summer.
